title: Greater Manchester mayor eyes derelict public land for council housing

input.lead: The mayor of Greater Manchester, Bev Craig, has issued a "call to action" to public bodies
input.summary: The mayor of Greater Manchester, Bev Craig, has issued a "call to action" to public bodies
input.evidence_text: Greater Manchester mayor eyes derelict public land for council housing - BBC News Image source, PA Media Image caption, Bev Craig wants Greater Manchester to lead the way in building a new generation of council houses By Mat Trewern and Richard Stead North West Published 12 August 2026 Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig has appealed to public sector bodies to "offer up" derelict land so tens of thousands of council houses can be built. The new mayor is aiming to build 10,000 "genuinely affordable" homes in the city region by May 2028, part of a longer-term plan to create 50,000 council and social houses. A "public sector land bank" is being created to find brownfield sites that will be given priority for building. The Home Builders Federation said the plan was welcome but that "similar ambitions had floundered" in the past. Image caption, Mayor Bev Craig says she has a clear but ambitious target for building new council houses The mayor said she wanted Greater Manchester to "lead the way in building a new generation" of council and social homes. "If you're sitting on a small piece of land that's surplus to requirement, then offer it into the pot and let's get building," Craig said. She said the target of 10,000 houses by 2028 was "ambitious", which was why she was "issuing a call to action" for public sector organisations. "I want to have a clear plan and I want us to get building", she said. "There are too many people waiting for a good home... too many people living in temporary accommodation", she added. She said council housing was a "safety net" and a "foundation for a good life". The mayor said she would use government grants towards paying for the homes. title: Trafford Council's adult social care 'requires improvement' - CQC

input.lead: Trafford Council says it remains committed to delivering further improvements to the service
input.summary: Trafford Council says it remains committed to delivering further improvements to the service
input.evidence_text: Trafford Council's adult social care 'requires improvement' - CQC - BBC News Image source, LDRS Image caption, Trafford Council's leader, Tom Ross, said it was important to recognise that the report reflected a service presently undergoing significant change By Angela Ferguson North West Published 12 August 2026 A council's adult social care provision "requires improvement", a report by a health and social care watchdog has found. The Care Quality Commission (CQC) found issues at Trafford Council, including people not always being able to access equipment and minor home adaptations in a timely manner, negatively impacting their independence. People were also found to have waited a long time for occupational therapy assessments. Jane Slater, Trafford Council's executive member for healthy and independent lives, said they welcomed the clarity provided by the assessment and "recognise the areas where further improvement is needed". "We have already seen considerable progress over the past year, but we know there is more to do," she said. The council's Adult Social Care provision supports thousands of residents, including older people, adults with disabilities, people with mental health needs, and unpaid carers. Mary Cridge, CQC's director of adult social care, said their assessment "found several areas where the local authority needed to make improvements to ensure people had good access to the adult social care and the support they needed". Cridge said it was encouraging to hear about the progress that had already been made, and the plans and strategies in place to continue improvements. Many of these items contain batteries and valuable materials that can be recover When electrical items are placed in black and brown bins, they can also become damaged during collection and processing. This can cause batteries to spark, leading to fires that put waste and recycling crews at risk and can cause significant damage to vehicles and facilities Councillor Paul Kenny, portfolio holder for planning, environmental services and transport, said: "We know that during periods of hot weather, fans are often essential items to help people cool down, but when these products reach the end of their life, they should never be thrown "Electrical items and batteries can cause fires if damaged, putting our collection crews and staff at risk. By taking unwanted electricals to the correct recycling point, residents can help protect our workers, reduce waste, and ensure valuable materials are recovered and reused

input.evidence_text: A beloved feature of Haigh Woodland Park is on track to make a glorious return this summer The Haigh land train is fuelled up and ready to transport visitors across the site, with regular journeys scheduled between the courtyard and Plantation Gates Land trains have been a key feature on the site throughout its recent history and families can also bring their pets for a ride to help them get around the Haigh estate It will be running throughout the summer holidays Councillor Chris Ready, cabinet portfolio holder for communities and neighbourhoods, said: “The return of the land train at Haigh Hall is something very close to my heart. As a young lad, I used the train regularly, and I am proud to say that I still live within walking distance “This is something residents have been looking forward to for decades, and I know how much it means to so many people across our borough. I am absolutely delighted that we have been able to help deliver this for our residents
